Unionization is something that is very important to working men and women across the first congressional district. So my background is first and foremost, my grandfather was a steel worker. My predecessor, Congressman Viscowski, has set the bar at a very high level of being a champion and advocate for working men and women. and union labor throughout Northwest Indiana. And so near and dear to my heart is making sure that we protect unions every single day. So this pro act, is something that we passed in the 117th Congress. It did pass last year. It also allows workers to stand together to form a union and to have the ability to use their collective voices for fair wages. Also what we always have to consider is safe work environments, trade unions and all unions put an emphasis on safety and making sure not only are things built on time on schedule but safely and that everyone who goes to a job returns home from that job. And so union labor also, something that I believe is near and dear to my heart. So I'm a freshman member of Congress, I get sworn in on January 3rd, I take an oath On January 6th, we have events happen the insurrection or the riots at the capitol. I only bring that up because consistently what I have been saying, and I mean this wholeheartedly, is that what I am here to do is to close that gap, chip away at that divide. So what was very, very clear was that there's a divide in our nation. And very often workers think that they're being left behind or feel that they're being left behind. And if we could focus on the middle class, if we can focus on workers when we talk about renewable energies and new economies, when we talk about American jobs plan or an infrastructure bill, if we're bringing American workers along and we have a by American provision, and we focus on the domestic steel and manufacturing. of what is going on in making sure that when we rebuild our roads, bridges, waterways, dams, water pipelines, infrastructure, our electricity grid that we bring workers along. If we do that, I believe that will chip away at the divide. So the PRO Act has a lot to do with giving unions the right to collectively bargain, to have fair elections, to put themselves in a position to regain ground that may have been taken away from unions' bargaining rights. over the last decade or so. You had mentioned Indiana and one of the first states to pass the right to work. So some might say, well, who might that impact? If you can go back in history, and I was there on the Indiana State Capitol stairs, there were over 15,000 men and women who showed up to protest the Right to Work Act, 15,000. The entire state capital was full of people on the outside and on the lawn and inside. And so we must remember that the middle class and working men and women and having the ability to have a fair wage is what's at stake. And so I'd be happy to have this discussion and dive into it, but that's a little bit of my perspective of where we come from. And as a member of Congress, how I view our labor unions in northwest Indiana.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
transcript: Well, you had mentioned the National Labor Relations Board and what that focuses on under the current law. It's unable to enforce its own orders. When an entity does not comply with the Board's orders, the National Labor Relations Board must seek enforcement through the U.S. Courts of Appeals. The bill would authorize the National Labor Relations Board to enforce its own orders requiring employers that failed to comply with the labor board to pay a civil monetary penalty up to $10,000 for each violation. And so what that does is it circumfence where people were going around the National Labor Relations Board in order to provide, instead of going to the courts, it has a direct violation. And so you had also mentioned the focus on the right to work and how that impacts. The right to work and ultimately I kind of want to go in a couple different areas, but I want to you know How the how we focused in Congress You know, we always have to keep in perspective COVID-19 and what we were under over the last year and a half. And there was a great deal of uncertainty in the workplace. A lot of the proactive had a lot to do with making sure OSHA was protecting workers because there were many essential workers were union labor that were out there on the roads and the bridges and the mills in the supermarkets in the classrooms. And so the PRO Act actually made sure that there was safe working conditions and that we were addressing COVID-19. And as a matter of priorities, we passed an apprenticeship program, early on in the legislative cycle in January, February, making sure that we put programming and resources towards apprenticeship programs so that we have a workforce that is developed and ready to go. throughout the United States and throughout North, Northwest Indiana, the first congressional district, putting our resources in there, making sure that it's accessible to women, making sure that it's accessible to minorities, making sure that it's accessible to those who want a job can prepare to be in the trades. I bring that up because the next thing we did is we passed the PROAC, making sure that we're protecting the middle class. And as we protect the middle class and we get them to work and they have the right to collectively bargain, they have the right to earn a fair wage, they have a right to safe working conditions, they have the right to a pension that is promised to them that they had put in for. So those things are extremely important because it was a matter of priority to make sure that we were doing that and immediately it was only a day apart we passed the rescue plan making sure that we were getting people a national strategic plan for people to get shots to be vaccinated making sure that dollars were spent on infrastructure and sent to the communities the school systems so that we could get kids back in school safely and making sure that we held up the economy. And so those are the things that were extremely important to us as a Congress and going forward now, now that we have the pro act and in passing the house, we have to make this law. This allows us to say that the working men and women without labor, you wouldn't have productivity, you wouldn't have goods, you wouldn't have the ability to have a return on your investment. So I think that you are absolutely correct. This is the time that the middle class needs to make gains. This is the time that the middle class needs to close the wage gap and do all that we can to be able to provide an equitable system for all of us and for the working men and women of the first congressional district. That is what I'm focused on and that is a very acute observation. So I have in my mind a clock that is ticking backwards. I know I have 24 months to have deliverables. I know that we have to be able to make sure that we pass the PRO Act. We pass the American Jobs Plan. We pass the infrastructure bill that will invest in our community. We bring back resources, programming resources to Northwest Indiana that puts people back to work. And then we allow private businesses to do what they do best, create jobs. If we have the waterways in northwest Indiana, the little cow, the county net rivers, the rivers that lead into the steel mills, the harbors, if we deepen those, if we clean those out and we allow bigger products or more iron ore to come in, that allows our steel mills to invest more and to be able to make more. And so that infrastructure, so now if the still mills are making more, we want them to share that with the workers, right? And if we invest in our infrastructure, people have to understand then what we are doing is we're investing in ourselves to be able to make more of a living. And that's the system that I believe in. And that's what I'm advocating for every single day.
